items.title: perf: benchmark matrix + pipeline decomposition + Cantera baseline
items.body:
## Summary

A performance benchmark suite for ChemMechSim.jl. Builds on the compile/warm principle discovered during this work: the dominant perf cost for large mechanisms is one-time Julia JIT compilation of the MTK-generated Jacobian codegen, NOT the linear-solver choice.

### New scripts
- **`bench_matrix.jl`** — mechanism × linear-solver benchmark matrix (GRI30/FFCM2/Aramco × 5 direct sparse solvers: KLU/UMFPACK/Sparspak/MUMPS/Pardiso). Separates one-time compile (`compile_probe`) from per-solver warm solve + standalone linsolve micro-bench + trajectory accuracy vs reference. Repeats with median + IQR statistics.
- **`plot_bench.py`** — renders warm e2e time, compile-vs-N, and per-call linsolve figures (publication rcParams).
- **`plot_pipeline.py`** — stacked-bar pipeline decomposition (build / JIT compile / warm integrate) per mechanism.
- **`cantera_baseline.py`** — external baseline: Cantera cold/warm solve on the same GRI30 + Aramco problems.
- **`gri30_benchmark.jl`** — refactored from GRI30-only to multi-mech pipeline decomposition (build → cold → warm → jit_compile).

### Key findings

1. **JIT compilation dominates and scales with mechanism size** (gri30 8s → ffcm2 32s → aramco 569s), while warm solve stays small (~0.2 / 2.3 / 10s). The linear-solver choice is NOT the bottleneck.

2. **The earlier "KLU 35× slower" finding was a measurement artifact.** KLU ran first in the prior probe and paid the shared Jacobian-codegen compile (~422s); UMFPACK ran second (compile done, 12s). Fresh-process KLU (402s) ≈ UMFPACK (401s) — both pay the same compile.

3. **MUMPS is the fastest warm solver (3.6s on Aramco) but produces INCORRECT results** (T diverges by 1415K). The accuracy-vs-reference check catches this — without it, MUMPS would be misidentified as the winner.

4. **ChemMechSim warm (9.5s KLU) is competitive with Cantera (5.3s)** on Aramco — ~1.8× slower. The gap is entirely the cold-start JIT compile cost (569s vs Cantera's 5.4s), inherent to the symbolic-codegen approach.

5. **The optimization lever is opaque registered functions** (shrink the generated code → less to compile), not the linear solver. PLOG is already opaque; K_c and species sums are the next targets.

### Verification
- 5-solver × 3-mech × 5-repeat matrix run with accuracy check (MUMPS flagged incorrect).
- Cantera baseline: GRI30 + Aramco cold/warm timed.
- Pipeline benchmark: build/cold/warm/jit_compile for all 3 mechs.
- Smoke-tested on gri30 (all paths: e2e, micro-bench, accuracy, compile probe, metadata).

### Scope
`examples/perf/` + `Project.toml` (MUMPS, Pardiso, LinearSolve, Sparspak deps). No framework `src/` changes.

items.title: v0.2.0: fix incorrect results, rewrite the kernels, and re-document
items.body:
## Summary

**v0.1.1 returned a single repeated value for every input** on any system with
NumPy 2.x. The CUDA kernels were computing correct values; the binding threw
them away. This PR fixes that, replaces the two hot kernels, and rebuilds the
packaging, tests, CI and documentation around them.

Verified on an RTX A6000 (sm_86, CUDA 12.5): 45 Python tests and 11 C++ tests
pass, `ruff` is clean, and a clean `pip install` from the tree works.

## The headline bug

`python/CMakeLists.txt` pinned pybind11 **v2.10.4**, which predates NumPy 2.0's
change to the array descriptor layout. Built against NumPy ≥ 2, every returned
array had a **stride of 0**, so all elements aliased element 0:

```
cuLOF   : 1 unique value;   [9.4945 9.4945 9.4945 9.4945 ...]
sklearn : 500 unique values; [9.4945 9.9042 8.9527 10.4107 ...]
```

The kernels were fine — the value being broadcast is the correct score for
point 0. CMake now requires pybind11 ≥ 2.12, and
`test_output_is_not_a_constant` guards the symptom.

## Other correctness fixes

- **Every build targeted sm_52.** `project(LANGUAGES CUDA)` seeds
  `CMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES`, so the detection function's `if(DEFINED ...)`
  guard always returned early — an sm_86 A6000 ran Maxwell code.
- **`normalize=True` was undefined behaviour**: `cudaMemcpyHostToDevice` on a
  device pointer, and `cudaHostRegister` on device memory.
- **Non-contiguous input silently gave wrong answers**: the binding checked only
  `strides[1]` before passing the raw pointer, so `X[::2]` was read as
  contiguous.
- `k > 32` raised `cudaErrorInvalidValue`; zero-variance features produced NaN
  under `normalize=True`; `--use_fast_math` contradicted the documented aim of
  matching scikit-learn; `BUILD_TESTS=ON` could not configure.

## Performance

Distances are now a single cuBLAS `SGEMM` via `‖a-b‖² = ‖a‖² + ‖b‖² - 2a·b` on
centred data, replacing an elementwise kernel that accumulated in float64 — a
1:64 rate on consumer Ampere.

k-NN is an exact **radix select on the raw float bit patterns**. LOF needs the
neighbour *set* and the k-distance, never their order, so selection suffices —
and the k-th key the select produces *is* the k-distance. No k limit, coalesced
reads, O(n) per pass. The Gram-to-distance conversion is fused into the first
pass and 11-bit digits cover 32 bits in three passes, so the tile is swept four
times rather than six.

The n×n matrix is no longer materialised; tiling keeps memory linear in n.
**n = 200,000 now runs where it previously needed 149 GiB.**

| samples | scikit-learn | cuLOF | speedup |
|--------:|-------------:|------:|--------:|
| 1,000   | 0.013 s | 0.0002 s | 63× |
| 20,000  | 0.717 s | 0.0221 s | 33× |
| 50,000  | 2.970 s | 0.0954 s | 31× |
| 200,000 | 16.93 s | 1.411 s  | 12× |

RTX A6000 vs 24-thread i9-12900K, k=20, best of 7, context init excluded.

## API

`LOF` is now a genuine drop-in for `sklearn.neighbors.LocalOutlierFactor` —
`n_neighbors`, `contamination`, `fit_predict` returning ±1 labels,
`score_samples`, `negative_outlier_factor_`, `offset_`. A test asserts label-for-label
equality with scikit-learn. `culof.lof(X, k)` returns the LOF value itself.

The previous `set_k`/`set_threshold` surface is gone, as is the pure-Python
`LOF` class that `__init__.py` defined and then immediately overwrote with the
C++ one — so the documented API never existed at runtime.

## Accuracy

Agreement is measured, not asserted: median relative difference **4.5×10⁻⁷**,
p99 2.4×10⁻⁶, identical top-1% rankings everywhere. The tail is points whose
k-th and (k+1)-th neighbours are closer than float32 can resolve, where the
choice of k-th neighbour is genuinely ambiguous; 0.27% of points, and it never
changed which points were flagged. `test_near_ties_are_the_only_disagreement`
pins this down rather than hiding it behind a loose tolerance.

## Everything else

- Packaging on `pyproject.toml` + scikit-build-core; `setup.py` gone; version has one source.
- Python package moved under `src/` so tests exercise the installed artefact, not the source tree.
- Removed the duplicated `python/` tree, which shipped a second copy of the tests and a top-level module named `python`.
- Deterministic output: the gather uses a block-wide prefix sum, not atomics, so runs are bit-identical.
- CI across CUDA 11.8/12.4 and Python 3.9–3.12.
- Figures are generated from the benchmark's own JSON. The old README and two figures carried three contradictory speedup numbers (6.75×, 4.6×, 1.57×).

## Note

The `.github/workflows/ci.yml` file needs a token with the `workflow` scope to
push over HTTPS; this branch was pushed over SSH.

items.title: fix: correct tail buffer selection in double-buffered SGEMM
items.body:
# Summary

Fix incorrect shared-memory buffer selection in the tail compute pass of the double-buffered SGEMM kernel.

## Problem

The tail pass always reads from shared-memory buffer `1`, but the final K-tile is written to buffer `(numTiles - 1) & 1`. This is only guaranteed to be buffer `1` when `numTiles` is even. For odd `numTiles`, the tail pass reads stale data from the wrong buffer, producing incorrect results.

## Fix

Compute the final buffer index once:
```c
int smem_sel_last = (((K + BK - 1) / BK) - 1) & 1;
```
and use it instead of the hardcoded buffer index in the tail compute loop.

## Testing

- Verified no regression for existing benchmark shapes (K = 2048, 4096, 8192).
- Verified correctness against torch.matmul for K = 2040 (numTiles = 255), where the previous implementation produced incorrect results.

items.title: fix(interp): make recursive trace boundary explicit
items.body:
## Summary

Fixes #184.

The Fannkuch compare benchmark could produce incorrect results in `default` and `jit` modes while `threaded` remained correct.

## Root cause

The trace recorder used `skipCall` when it encountered a recursive `CALL`. That is only sound when the recorder can model the call's effects. `skipCall` supplies placeholder return values and does not reproduce the callee's heap mutations.

A recursive call encountered inside a non-entry loop trace could therefore leave the recorder with a speculative VM/heap state that never existed. Fannkuch exposes this because its recursive permutation routine mutates a shared array and continues execution after the call.

## Fix

Treat recursive calls in non-entry loop traces as a trace boundary. The native prefix is retained, the real recursive call executes through the threaded path, and the post-call continuation can be captured from the actual frame and heap state.

Function-entry self-recursion keeps the existing native `selfCall` path, so the fix does not disable native recursive-call lowering globally or reject heap mutation from JIT plans.

The JIT trace contract documentation is updated to describe the boundary explicitly.

## Validation

- `go test -race ./...`
- `go vet ./...`
- `go test -tags=compare -run='^$' -bench='^BenchmarkCall_Fannkuch$' -benchtime=1x -count=5`
- `git diff --check`

The Fannkuch compare benchmark passes for `default`, `threaded`, `jit`, `native`, `gpython`, and `cpython` on the ARM64 development machine.

items.title: fix(benchmark): capture warmup end time before benchmark phase
items.body:
## Bug
Warmup duration in benchmark results was incorrect. It showed ~5500 ms for `--benchmark-fast` (500ms warmup + 5000ms benchmark + processing). The reported warmup time included the entire benchmark phase.

## Root cause
`warmup_duration_ms` was calculated as:
```c
result->warmup_duration_ms = (int)(get_microseconds() - warmup_start) / 1000;
```
But `get_microseconds()` was called at line 156, **after** the benchmark phase completed. So it captured warmup + benchmark + result processing time.

## Fix
Capture `warmup_end = get_microseconds()` immediately after the warmup loop ends (line 110), before the benchmark phase starts. Use `warmup_end - warmup_start` for the warmup duration report.

## Before/After
| | Warmup reported | Actual warmup |
|---|---|---|
| Before | ~5501 ms | 500 ms |
| After | 500 ms | 500 ms |

**Do not merge without explicit approval.**

items.body:
### What problem does this PR solve?
Issue Number: close #785 

This PR fixes Spark SQL timestamp parsing behavior around time zone conversion, especially for daylight saving time (DST) gaps and historical `Asia/Shanghai` transitions.

Before this change, `unix_timestamp` / `to_unix_timestamp` / `get_timestamp` could return incorrect results for local timestamps that fall into DST gaps or ambiguous transition periods. Some invalid or unsupported timestamp values, such as negative years, were also not consistently converted to `NULL` as expected by Spark-compatible behavior.

### Type of Change

### Description
This PR updates Spark SQL timestamp-to-GMT conversion logic to better match Spark/JVM behavior.

Main changes:

- Added a shared GMT conversion helper that handles:
  - fixed-offset time zones,
  - named TZ time zones,
  - nonexistent local timestamps during DST gaps,
  - ambiguous local timestamps during DST fallback transitions,
  - out-of-range timestamp values.

- Updated `unix_timestamp` and `get_timestamp` conversion paths to return `NULL` instead of throwing or producing incorrect results when the parsed timestamp cannot be represented or should be treated as nonexistent.

- Fixed Spark-compatible behavior for DST gaps:

  - For regular named time zones such as `America/Los_Angeles` and `Europe/Berlin`, nonexistent local timestamps are shifted forward using Spark/JVM-compatible semantics.

items.title: [spsm] Fix matrix initialization for sparse triangular solve
items.body:
The benchmark uses `init_matrix()` to initialize a general sparse matrix, but `{cu,hip}sparseSpSM_solve` expect a triangular matrix. `init_matrix()` doesn't satisfy the required preconditions, which may lead to incorrect results, as shown below.

```
./main 20082 128 150616 100 1
Initializing host matrices..
Done
Average execution time of SpSM solve: 223.996048 (us)
Checking results..
@9216 1.324598 != 0.000000
spsm_csr_example test FAILED: wrong result
```

There are two main issues:
1. Upper-triangular entries in the CSR. `init_matrix()` distributes non-zeros across the entire matrix, but then the benchmark uses `HIPSPARSE_FILL_MODE_LOWER`, which assumes that it will only contain lower-triangular entries. Note that the host-side reference `spsm()` in utils.h correctly uses only the lower triangle thanks to `if (k < i+1)`. 
2. Zero diagonal entries. The benchmark uses `HIPSPARSE_DIAG_TYPE_NON_UNIT`, which makes the solver use the actual diagonal values. However, at low density (make run default params: M=20082, nnz=150616 gives ~0.04% density), most of the diagonal entries are zero. 

This PR adds `init_lower_triangular_matrix()` to utils.h, which directly generates a lower-triangular sparse matrix with guaranteed non-zero diagonal entries. Both the CUDA and HIP variants are updated to use it.

items.title: OA-first Risk-of-Bias benchmark — Stage A (expert-labelled OA core)
items.body:
## Why

Previous studies produced incorrect results because of how trial full text was sourced. Both failures traced to the same root cause — **starting from a fixed target trial and then trying to fetch it**: when the target is paywalled, the pipeline either misses it (the 9 unrecoverable EM regional-journal RCTs) or *silently substitutes the wrong document* (RCT030 grabbing its parent Cochrane review; the earlier Cochrane harvest binding ratings to a conference-proceedings book — see `docs/papers/drafts/medrxiv_V5/FORENSICS.md`).

**The fix is to invert the sourcing:** enumerate the *open-access* population first and admit a trial only when its full text is genuinely in hand **and** it carries a verified human-expert RoB 2 label. Open access becomes a construction guarantee, not a hope — there is no paywalled target left to substitute.

Design spec: `docs/superpowers/specs/2026-07-17-oa-first-rob-benchmark-design.md`
Plan: `docs/superpowers/plans/2026-07-17-oa-rob-benchmark-stage-a.md`

## What this PR contains (Stage A — the trusted, publishable OA core)

Every benchmark item must pass a four-part **litmus test**: (1) PMC-OA-subset full text with a redistributable license; (2) a complete six-field human-expert RoB 2 tuple in the canonical vocabulary `low`/`some concerns`/`high`; (3) verified trial↔label linkage + trial-compatible PublicationType; (4) recorded provenance + license. Labels are stored **as data + citation**, never as source-review prose (so the result is publishable even when the source review is subscription-access).

Two new shared collectors:
- `biasbuster/collectors/oa_license.py` — PMC-OA-subset + license resolver (CC/CC0 → redistributable; NC/ND flagged per item).
- `biasbuster/collectors/study_pmid_resolver.py` — **clean** study→PMID resolver (bracket-ref or author+year+title-similarity ≥0.70). No surname-only, no "first-of-many" — the two anti-patterns that corrupted the earlier corpus are structurally absent.

New study package `studies/oa_rob_benchmark/`:
- `rob2_tuple.py` — six-field tuple assembler (structural-table path + ROBoto2 signalling-answer path via the existing RoB 2 algorithm).
- `store.py` — isolated SQLite store (`dataset/oa_rob_benchmark.db`) enforcing the litmus test; append/upsert only, never DROP; never touches `biasbuster.db` or the EM benchmark DB.
- `ingest_roboto2.py` — Stage A seed pool 1 (ROBoto2's 245 human-expert RoB 2 rows; LLM-assisted rows dropped).
- `ingest_em_candidates.py` + `jats_refs.py` — Stage A seed pool 2 (EM OA trials, labels **re-derived** from the primary reviews, not copied from EM's gated supplement; **RCT030 excluded**).
- `manual_gate.py` — 20-row manual-check manifest generator (the mandatory pre-scaling gate).
- `export.py` — redistributable export (identifiers + license + tuple + provenance; NC/ND flagged; local cache paths excluded).
- `scripts/audit_oa_rob_benchmark.py` — re-checks all four litmus rules across the finished DB, sharing the store's single `litmus_violations` source of truth.

Reuses existing infrastructure unchanged: `rob_table_extractor`, `pubtype`, `retry`, `cochrane_rob2/algorithms`, and the Europe PMC JATS fetch.

## Quality

Built task-by-task with a fresh implementer + independent reviewer per task. Reviews caught and fixed two real correctness bugs: a worst-wins vocabulary mismatch that silently downgraded `some concerns`→`low`, and a `WRONG_PAPER_RCTS` keying bug that would have let RCT030's trial through the exclusion. Final whole-branch review: **no Critical/Important findings**; RCT030 exclusion verified structurally effective. **627 tests pass** (43 new across the 8 Stage A test files).

## Owner actions before the real data lands (not code — flagged in the spec)

- Confirm ROBoto2 label-reuse terms with its authors before *publishing* ROBoto2-derived rows (spec risk R1).
- Place the ROBoto2 dataset file, then run the ingests from your terminal (they perform network I/O over the full cohort — kept out of CI per the >2-min rule): `uv run python -m studies.oa_rob_benchmark.ingest_roboto2` and `... ingest_em_candidates`.
- Review the 20-row manual-gate manifest (≥19/20 must match) before Stage B (the fresh OA-first harvest) is planned.

## Deferred, non-blocking (tracked for a follow-up)
- Blank-string signalling values aren't caught by the missing-domain guard (backstopped by the manual gate).
- `trial_pmcid` stored raw vs PMC-normalized; a same-author/same-year multi-candidate resolver regression test.
- Owner sign-off on shipping broad provenance fields in the published export.

## The defect

`XLStyleValue.GetTransition` matched cache entries on a 32-bit hash of the component key and never compared the key itself. Two distinct keys sharing a hash returned each other's style, so a cell silently ended up with a number format, font or border it was never assigned.

The doc comment claimed *"collisions simply evict"*. That holds for **slot** collisions (different hash, same slot) but not for **hash** collisions, which return the wrong entry.

## It is reachable through the public API

Not theoretical. A custom number format pins `NumberFormatId` to a constant `-1`, so the key's hash reduces to `string.GetHashCode(Format)`. A birthday search finds a colliding pair of ordinary-looking format strings among ~2^16 candidates in **62 ms**:

```
A = "#,##0.00_);[Red](57956)"    hash=-1411878033
B = "#,##0.00_);[Red](104231)"   hash=-1411878033

cell B expected "#,##0.00_);[Red](104231)"
cell B actual   "#,##0.00_);[Red](57956)"     <-- silently took cell A's format
```

For a workbook applying *k* distinct custom formats to default-styled cells the odds run near `k²/2³³` — roughly **1 in 8,000 at k = 1,000**. `XLFontKey` carries a font name and is exposed the same way.

Worst property: `string.GetHashCode()` is randomised per process, so an unchanged workbook round-trips correctly on most runs and corrupts on others, with nothing in the file to explain it.

## Scope — what is *not* affected

A brute force over **11.4M `XLAlignmentKey` values**, spanning Excel's full permitted `Indent` / `RelativeIndent` / `TextRotation` ranges, found **zero collisions**. The record-struct hash is linear in those `int` fields, so a collision needs a short lattice vector that does not exist in that box.

Only the string-bearing keys were ever exposed. Recorded here so nobody re-audits the int-keyed components.

## The fix

The cache now holds `(hash, component key, result)` and compares the key on every hit. The hash stays as the cheap reject, so the miss path is unchanged; a hit adds a type test and a struct compare. Boxing falls only on a **store** — one per distinct transition per base style, not per cell.

Two things noticed while in here:

- **`ModifyFont` used the raw hash** while the other five tagged theirs, despite the comment claiming the tag prevents cross-component collisions. Made uniform; the type test in `GetTransition` is what actually rejects those now.
- **`StoreTransition` publishes the hash last** via `Volatile.Write`. The hash is what a lookup gates on, so a concurrent reader either misses or sees a fully written entry — preserving the *"benign races cause at most a miss, never incorrect results"* property that adding a second field would otherwise have broken.

## Verification

- Regression test added to `XLStyleValueTests`; **fails before the fix, passes after**. The colliding pair is searched for at run time rather than hard-coded, because per-process hash randomisation means no literal pair collides on every run.
- **11,832 tests pass**, 4 skipped (pre-existing).

Performance A/B on `CellStylingBenchmarks` (100,000 rows), library-only change with the benchmark binary identical across arms:

| Benchmark | before | after |
|---|---:|---:|
| `ValueOnly` | 25.57 ms | 24.90 ms |
| `StyleFacadePerCell` | 48.41 ms | 45.75 ms |
| `StyleAssignedPerCell` | 45.15 ms | 42.40 ms |
| `TwoPropertiesPerCell` | 61.93 ms | 61.76 ms |
| `FacadeStyleOnly` | 46.16 ms | 42.61 ms |
| `FacadeChainOnly` | 49.20 ms | 39.35 ms |
| `StyleOnColumn` | 19.57 ms | 18.18 ms |

**Allocation is byte-identical across all seven variants** (37.83 / 37.07 / 43.17 / 32.49 / 35.54 / 16.25 / 24.86 MB), which is the exact evidence that the boxing stays off the hot path.

The times should be read as *no measurable regression*, not as an improvement: every variant moved the same direction, including `FacadeStyleOnly` and `FacadeChainOnly`, which never call a façade setter and cannot be reached by this change. Uniform non-directional movement in unreachable variants is machine drift.

## Notes

- No public API change.
- Branched from `main`; independent of the open perf PR (#perf/template-round-trip), whose spec 18 carries the "deserves its own issue" note that this resolves.

## Summary

- Add an engine `--proof-extraction` mode that follows strict proof testing through check rewriting, proof extraction, materialization, cleanup, and simplification, but skips the two proof-verifier passes.

items.title: Topic 10: Hashing, checksums, and PRNG selection
items.body: ## Summary - add Topic 10's contract-first selection guide for hashes, checksums, CRCs, and PRNGs - implement independent bitwise, slice-by-one table, and runtime-dispatched hardware CRC-32C paths - add correctness checks, a harness-free process benchmark, codegen inspection, and strict evidence validation - preserve exact-source Arm and x86-64 results from 12 order-balanced process pairs per host ## Focused result - source candidate: `2ef02391a7f2e68587cbf8f18494b73331f9a4d8` - source archive SHA-256: `3b0c06b53e402bf9bb74ac24da77e326419607f9f37af47b7ca3a78e45d91598` - Arm paired hardware speedup median: 54.830x, MAD 0.081x - x86-64 paired hardware speedup median: 21.886x, MAD 0.011x - scope: one warmed 4 KiB CRC-32C slice, bytewise table versus one dependent dedicated-instruction chain ## Primary sources - Rust `HashMap` and hashing contracts - CRC RevEng CRC-32C and CRC-32/ISO-HDLC parameter catalogues - Intel SSE4.2 and Arm ACLE CRC instruction contracts - Blackman and Vigna PRNG analysis, Random123, Rust Rand reproducibility guidance, and Lemire bounded sampling Direct links are in `topics/010-hashing-checksums-prng/references.md`. ## Validation - `git diff --check` - `cargo fmt --all -- --check` - `cargo test --workspace --lib --examples` - `cargo test --workspace --doc` - `cargo clippy --workspace --all-targets -- -D warnings` - `cargo bench --workspace --no-run` - `RUSTDOCFLAGS='-D warnings' cargo doc --workspace --no-deps` - exact-source correctness, benchmark verification, linked-binary disassembly, and the same gates on both required Linux hosts - `shasum -a 256 -c topics/010-hashing-checksums-prng/measurements/raw/2ef0239/SHA256SUMS` All listed gates passed. The draft does not merge or publish the lesson. This adds Topic 10’s contract-first guide and a complete CRC-32C study covering portable, table-driven, and runtime-selected hardware implementations. Before this, the curriculum had no material or reproducible evidence for choosing among hashes, checksums, CRCs, and PRNGs; the new topic supplies correctness checks, benchmarks, provenance validation, and cross-host measurements. ## Why it was needed Hashing, checksumming, CRC, and PRNG APIs are not interchangeable: selecting an implementation before fixing the algorithm and compatibility contract can produce incorrect results. The topic establishes the CRC-32C/Castagnoli contract, distinguishes it from CRC-32/ISO-HDLC, and records evidence for the performance trade-off between portable and hardware paths. ## How it works 1. `src/lib.rs` defines CRC polynomial constants, bitwise reference implementations, a compile-time slice-by-one table, and CRC-32C hardware dispatch for x86-64 and AArch64. 2. `Crc32cKernel` selects the table or detected hardware implementation while preserving common update and finalization semantics. 3. `check_equivalence.rs` compares implementations against known vectors, tests offsets and boundary lengths, and verifies fragmented updates equal whole-slice updates. 4. `benches/crc32c.rs` performs warmed, deterministic whole-slice measurements while excluding setup, allocation, dispatch selection, and correctness checks from the timed region. 5. `run_processes.sh` validates source provenance, archive digests, build gates, benchmark artifacts, disassembly, and architecture-specific instructions before collecting measurements. 6. `summarize.py` rejects malformed or unbalanced records, validates checksums and timing fields, then computes paired speedups and dispersion. 7. The recorded reports preserve host, toolchain, source, binary, checksum, and raw process evidence for Arm and x86-64 runs. The experiment uses 12 order-balanced pairs per host and measures a warmed 4 KiB CRC-32C slice. Reported median hardware speedups are 54.830× on Arm and 21.886× on x86-64. ## Key decisions - The independent bitwise implementation acts as the correctness oracle for table and hardware paths. - Runtime feature detection provides hardware acceleration where supported while retaining a portable fallback. - Fresh-process paired runs reduce persistent process-state effects and alternate execution order to limit ordering bias. - Exact source archives, SHA-256 manifests, binary hashes, symbols, and disassembly make the measurements auditable. - The benchmark intentionally measures steady-state checksum work, not allocation, input construction, dispatch, or process startup. - The lesson remains unpublished and does not alter the curriculum beyond registering the new session. ## Review focus - Verify CRC initialization, reflection, finalization, and update semantics remain identical across all kernels. - Check architecture-specific feature detection and intrinsic paths fall back safely when hardware support is unavailable. - Review benchmark validation invariants, especially byte counts, checksum/digest agreement, pair ordering, and hexadecimal fields. - Confirm provenance checks reject mismatched Git trees, archives, and source digests. - Treat the reported speedups as scoped evidence for the warmed 4 KiB workload, not general-purpose performance claims. ## Files | Area | Files | |---|---| | Curriculum and package setup | `curriculum.toml`, `topics/010-hashing-checksums-prng/Cargo.toml` | | Documentation | `topics/010-hashing-checksums-prng/README.md`, `topics/010-hashing-checksums-prng/rounds/01.md`, `topics/010-hashing-checksums-prng/references.md` | | CRC implementation | `topics/010-hashing-checksums-prng/src/lib.rs` | | Correctness example | `topics/010-hashing-checksums-prng/examples/check_equivalence.rs` | | Benchmark | `topics/010-hashing-checksums-prng/benches/crc32c.rs` | | Experiment runner | `topics/010-hashing-checksums-prng/experiment/run_processes.sh` | | Result validation and summarization | `topics/010-hashing-checksums-prng/experiment/summarize.py` | | Measurement reports | `topics/010-hashing-checksums-prng/measurements/2026-07-20-cross-host.md`, `2026-07-20-dev-dsk-ahrav-2b.md`, `2026-07-20-xlg.md`, `measurements/README.md` | | Raw evidence | `topics/010-hashing-checksums-prng/measurements/raw/2ef0239/` and its host-specific manifests, logs, binaries, checksums, environment captures, and disassembly |

items.title: Fix macOS 26 broken CIS benchmark policy queries
items.body:
Relates to #35120

## Summary

Eleven policy queries in the macOS 26 CIS v1.0.0 benchmark fail or produce incorrect results due to macOS 26 architecture changes. All fixes are confined to `ee/cis/macos-26/cis-policy-queries.yml`.

| CIS ID | Policy | Root Cause | Change |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2.3.3.1 | Screen Sharing Is Disabled | macOS 26 socket activation: `com.apple.screensharing` appears in `launchd` table when sharing is **off**, not on — logic inverted | Replace `launchd WHERE label = 'com.apple.screensharing'` with `listening_ports WHERE port = 5900` |
| 2.3.3.2 | File Sharing Is Disabled | Same socket activation inversion — `com.apple.smbd` entry behavior reversed | Replace `launchd WHERE label = 'com.apple.smbd'` with `listening_ports WHERE port = 445` |
| 2.3.3.4 | Remote Login Is Disabled | Same socket activation inversion — `com.openssh.sshd` entry behavior reversed | Replace `launchd WHERE label = 'com.openssh.sshd'` with `listening_ports WHERE port = 22` |
| 2.3.3.6 | Remote Apple Events Is Disabled | Same socket activation inversion — `com.apple.AEServer` entry behavior reversed | Replace `launchd WHERE label = 'com.apple.AEServer'` with `listening_ports WHERE port = 3031` |
| 2.3.3.7 | Internet Sharing Is Disabled | `com.apple.nat` plist nests `Enabled` inside a `NAT` dictionary; `key = 'Enabled'` never matches at the top level on macOS 26 | Replace `plist` check with `sharing_preferences WHERE internet_sharing = 1` |
| 2.3.3.10 | Bluetooth Sharing Is Disabled | `com.apple.Bluetooth` plist does not exist on macOS 26; `preferences` table returns no rows regardless of sharing state | Replace `preferences` check with `sharing_preferences WHERE bluetooth_sharing = 1` |
| 2.3.4.2 | Time Machine Volumes Are Encrypted | Previous query checked `value = 'NotEncrypted'` in the `plist` table which never matches on macOS 26; macOS 26 changed the `AutoBackup` boolean from `'1'` to `'true'` | Rewrite to check `preferences WHERE key = 'AutoBackup' AND value = 'true'` (TM enabled), pass if TM disabled or if an encrypted volume is mounted |
| 5.2.2 | Password Minimum Length | macOS 26 `pwpolicy` creates identifier `com.apple.policy.legacy.minChars`; query filters on `%minLength` which never matches | Rewrite to use `JSON_EXTRACT(policy_parameters, '$.minimumLength')` with `policy_identifier LIKE '%minChars'` |
| 5.7 | Admin Cannot Unlock Locked Session | `LIKE '%authenticate-session-owner%'` matches both `authenticate-session-owner` (secure) and `authenticate-session-owner-or-admin` (insecure) — query can never fail | Add `AND rule NOT LIKE '%authenticate-session-owner-or-admin%'` |
| 5.10 | XProtect Is Running and Updated | `launchd` table on macOS 26 reads plist files from disk, not live service state — both entries always present regardless of whether XProtect is running | Replace `launchd` COUNT check with `processes WHERE name IN ('xprotectd', 'XProtectPluginService')` |
| 5.11 | Logging Is Enabled for Sudo | `sudo_info` JSON stores boolean flags as `null` (sudo -V prints key name with no value); query checks for `'true'`/`'1'` which never matches | Use `json_type(...) IS NOT NULL` to detect key presence vs absence |

items.title: [KernelGen][Iluvatar] Fix var_correction: accuracy_fail
items.body:
## Summary
- **Operator:** var_correction
- **Error type:** accuracy_fail
- **Root cause:** The shared var_welford_kernel uses tl.reduce with a custom Welford combine function to merge partial results across BLOCK_N chunks. On the Iluvatar backend, this pattern produces NaN values when BLOCK_M > 1, and Triton kernel specialization causes compiled kernels to produce incorrect results when reused with different M/N values across sequential calls.

items.title: wasm backend: PR #691 review follow-ups (GuardSubclass width, IntSignext/indexed-GC decline, bridge-iter journal root)
items.body:
Follow-up fixes from the Codex/CodeRabbit review of the (now-merged) #691, verified against current `main`.

## Commits
1. **wasm: correct GuardSubclass field width; decline runtime IntSignext and indexed GC ops** — three `majit-backend-wasm/src/codegen.rs` fixes:
   - `GuardSubclass` read `subclassrange_min` at `size_of::<usize>()` (4 bytes on wasm32); `PyType::subclassrange_min` is `AtomicI64`, so read 8 bytes on both the vtable and gcremovetypeptr paths.
   - `IntSignext` with a non-constant `num_bytes` operand aborted via `panic!`; a non-constant width is a valid IR shape (the cranelift backend resolves `arg(1)` at runtime), so return `BackendError::Unsupported` for interpreter fallback.

2. **jit: root the FBW bridge iterator cursor journal** — `FBW_BRIDGE_ITER_JOURNAL` held range-iterator refs across an authoritative bridge walk but was visited by no root walker, unlike its five sibling FBW journals. 3. **check.py: report exec times and true ratio in perf-gate FAIL lines** — the FAIL line printed raw run times and the gate threshold formatted as if it were the measured ratio. Print the startup-subtracted exec times the gate actually compared, their ratio, and the threshold.

items.title: Fix MX F4 GEMM  bugs on gfx1250
items.body:
JIRA ID : AIHPBLAS-1594
related to [AIHPBLAS-1594]
## Motivation

 Fix multiple bugs related to MX F4 (microscaling FP4) GEMM support on gfx1250, enabling correct MX F4 kernel generation, benchmarking, and validation.

## Technical Details

 Bug fixes:

  1. Fix MX data type errors when DepthU = 4 × MI-K. TDM load ordering with LDS double-buffering (SIA.py): MX scale (MXSA/MXSB) tensor_load_to_lds instructions were not deferred past the LDS swap like A/B loads. This caused MX scale data to land in the wrong LDS bank, leading to mismatched scale and data reads during compute. Fixed by splitting and deferring MX scale TDM loads alongside their corresponding A/B loads. Adjusted a problem size (1024 → 1536) to cover the DU = 4×MI-K case
  2. Remove unnecessary VGPR bank-conflict padding for WMMA_V3 (KernelWriter.py): The VGPR padding to avoid bank conflicts between VgprA and VgprC is not needed for WMMA_V3 (gfx1250), where A and C are loaded in different cycles. Removing this padding saves VGPRs.
  3. Reject SourceSwap for non-square MatrixInstruction (Solution.py): Non-square matrix instructions (e.g., 32x16 for MX F4) do not support SourceSwap. Added explicit rejection to prevent silent incorrect results.
  4. Fix assembly generation when DisableAsmComments is True (mxf4_gfx1250.yaml): The matrix_fmt modifier parser used find(' ') to delimit the value, which failed when the modifier was followed by a tab or newline instead of a space. Changed to find_first_of(" \t\n\r").

items.title: Filter compound history queries by exact commit candidates
items.body:
## Goal

Resolve #73 by allowing application-owned semantic projections to constrain the generic Git-history query before relevance ranking/newest-first ordering and the final result limit.

## Scope

- [x] Add an optional exact object-ID restriction to `CommitHistoryQuery`.
- [x] Preserve the distinction between no restriction and an explicitly empty candidate set.
- [x] Trim, deduplicate and defensively copy candidate IDs.
- [x] Apply candidates as a Hibernate Search `terms` filter in the full-text path.
- [x] Apply candidates through the same HQL selection in the structured path.
- [x] Keep candidate membership score-neutral.
- [x] Add query-contract tests for omission, empty candidates, normalization, deduplication and immutability.
- [x] Add H2 integration evidence for full-text composition, structured composition, limiting after candidate filtering and empty-set behavior.
- [x] Document the cross-projection candidate-plan pattern.
- [x] Run Java CI, JGit compatibility and benchmark workflows.

## Correctness boundary

This API prevents the incorrect pattern:

```text
limited generic results ∩ limited semantic results
```

Instead:

```text
unlimited exact semantic candidate IDs
  -> generic compound query filter
  -> generic ranking/order
  -> final limit
```

The generic projection still owns only Git facts. Domain semantics and branch membership remain in the consuming application.

## Compatibility

Existing callers that do not invoke `restrictedToObjectIds(...)` retain unchanged query behavior. Passing an empty collection is intentionally match-none, not equivalent to omitting the restriction.

- Java CI with PostgreSQL/Testcontainers: passed.
- JGit 7.5, 7.6 and 7.7 compatibility: passed.

#  Arcus 5.0.0

All notable changes to Arcus are documented here.
This project adheres to [Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/).

## Added

- .NET 10 (`net10.0`) target framework
- `IIPAddressRange.ToIPAddresses()` -- safe enumeration method capped at `MaxEnumerationExponent`
- `MaxEnumerationExponent` property on all range types (default 12 = 4096 addresses)

- Regex source generators for improved parsing performance
- Partial class split for maintainability (`Subnet`, `IPAddressRange`, `AbstractIPAddressRange`, `BigEndianBitWrapper`)

## Changed

- `SubnetUtilities.PrivateIPAddressRangesList` and `LinkLocalIPAddressRangesList` are now `readonly` (lazily initialized)
- `AbstractIPAddressRange.Overlaps` -- symmetry restored (both directions now return `true`)
- `IPAddressRange.TryExcludeAll` -- boundary guards at family min/max (no longer throws)
- `Subnet` parsing and `IPAddressUtilities` parsing use `[GeneratedRegex]` where available
- Package dependencies updated and centralized via `Directory.Packages.props`
- Deterministic builds enabled
- Language version set to C# 14
- XML documentation improved throughout all public APIs with RFC references
- Exception types corrected (`InvalidOperationException` to `ArgumentException` where appropriate)

## Removed

- `MacAddress` type (was `[Obsolete]` in v3.x) - replacement coming soon-ish in a new package
- `DefaultIPAddressRangeComparer` (use `DefaultIIPAddressRangeComparer`)
- Drops [Gulliver](https://github.com/sandialabs/gulliver) dependency

## Fixed

- `AbstractIPAddressRange.Overlaps` asymmetry (inner.Overlaps(outer) returned `false`)
- `ContainsAnyPrivateAddresses`/`ContainsAllPublicAddresses` endpoint heuristic producing incorrect results for ranges spanning private subnets
- `IPAddressRange.TryExcludeAll` throwing `InvalidOperationException` at family max address
- IComparable consistency across range types

## Deprecated (will be removed in future major version)

- `GetEnumerator()` on any range type -- use `ToIPAddresses()` instead
- `IIPAddressRange` implementing `IEnumerable<IPAddress>` -- use `ToIPAddresses()` explicitly
- `Subnet.TryIPv6FromPartial(string, out IEnumerable<Subnet>)` -- to be replaced / improved by more explicit methods

## Testing

- Comprehensive test suite expansion across all range types, comparers, converters, math, and utilities
- `Subnet` tests split into partial files: factory, `IComparable`, `IEquatable`, `ISerializable`, operators
- `IPAddressRange` tests split into partial files: factory, `IComparable`, `IEquatable`, `ISerializable`, operators

- Smoke test project (`smoketests/`) validating the packed NuGet package on real runtimes

## Infrastructure

- Benchmark project (`src/Arcus.Benchmarks/`) with BenchmarkDotNet for all major types
- CI/CD pipeline rework: build, CodeQL, dependency review, OpenSSF Scorecard, and smoke-test workflows
- `.slnx` solution format (replaces legacy `.sln`)

items.title: Repair control architecture and numerical contracts
items.body:
## Summary

- correct `ModelArray` stacking to preserve array rank and add explicit flattening concatenation
- distinguish sampled passivity evidence from analytic certification, including DC/Nyquist-aware grids and MIMO Hermitian checks
- replace state-index modal slicing with real-Schur ordering, conjugate-block preservation, Sylvester separation, and projection bases
- update the Gonum fork dependency from `v0.17.6-fork` to the latest published `v0.17.7-fork`
- assemble physical across/through constraints into descriptor dynamics with explicit channel bindings and grounded reaction variables
- bind generalized analysis points to plant-input or plant-output loop topology
- evaluate tuning goals against their intended response, frequency band, dynamic weights, and MIMO induced 2-norm
- expose the bounded Cartesian engine as `GridTune`, with `Systune` and `Looptune` retained as compatibility wrappers
- synchronize the API audit and generated architecture diagrams

## Why

Several APIs exposed shallow or ambiguous contracts: stacking silently flattened model grids, passivity sampling looked like certification, modal truncation depended on the current state basis, physical connections only combined metadata, and all named loop points and gain goals collapsed onto the same response. Those behaviors could produce plausible but mathematically incorrect results.

The revised modules own their invariants and workflows: model arrays own shape semantics, passivity results own their evidence status and grid, modal reduction owns Schur-block selection and projection, physical assembly owns topology and constraints, and tuning goals own point/response/grid/weight selection.

## Compatibility and impact

- `Passive` remains as a deprecated compatibility alias for `SampledPassive`.
- `ConcatModelArrays` provides the former flatten-and-append behavior explicitly.
- the original generalized-loop analysis point remains a plant-output break, preserving the prior `P*C` convention
- `Systune` and `Looptune` remain available and delegate to `GridTune`
- descriptor frequency responses now evaluate `C(sE-A)^{-1}B+D`
- correctness-oriented modal, physical-assembly, and MIMO tuning paths perform more work than the former simplified implementations
- passivity frequency grids (explicit or FRD) must now be strictly increasing, finite, non-negative, and at or below the Nyquist frequency for sampled models
- `ModalTruncate` now reports an explicit error when a requested order splits a complex-conjugate pair or a `MaxRealPart` threshold selects no modes, instead of silently falling back
- review follow-up: grid-search candidates no longer share the analysis-point map with the source model, and weighted-gain evaluation reuses buffers across the frequency loop (-30% allocations on the dynamic-weight path)

## Validation

- `go fix ./...`
- `go vet ./...`
- `go test -v -count=1 ./...`
- `go test -race -count=1 ./...`
- `go test -run '^$' -bench=. -benchmem -count=1 ./...` (315.1 s, PASS)
- clean workspace diagnostics
- persistent non-symmetric, similarity-invariance, conjugate-pair, descriptor-oracle, physical-network, point-topology, MIMO singular-value, weighted-band, and search-limit regression tests

Focused tuning benchmarks show the true point-aware induced-norm checks increase runtime while reducing allocations; the Cartesian search now has an explicit `MaxEvaluations` bound.

## CI follow-up

The initial Linux/amd64 run exposed an architecture-dependent logarithmic-grid endpoint rounding difference. Commit `9040de6` makes the generated passivity grid explicitly own its lower and Nyquist endpoints. Native arm64, Darwin amd64, full local race tests, both GitHub test jobs, and both downstream-consumer jobs now pass.

items.title: Speed up reference resolution with pure Python optimizations
items.body:
## Summary

Alternative approach to #168 — achieves massive speedup without requiring a C extension, keeping the codebase pure Python and easier to maintain.

### Three layers of optimization

**1. Resolved-reference cache + optimized iterators**
- `RefResolver._dereference` memoizes previously resolved `$ref` targets — the single biggest win for specs with shared refs
- Stack-based `reference_iterator` with concrete type checks instead of recursive generators
- Iterative `path_get`/`path_set` with `dict`/`list` fast paths, ABC fallback for exotic types
- `orjson` as optional fast deepcopy backend (`pip install prance[fast]`)
- Bug fix: `path_get` returned `defaultvalue` for falsy values like `0`, `[]`, `{}`

**2. Structural sharing for O(N) resolution**
- `_dereference` returns shared Python object references from cache instead of deep copies
- `_resolve_partial` uses direct in-place replacement via `_replace_at_path`
- Eliminates the O(N^2) blowup on chained `$ref` targets entirely
- Optional `materialize=True` parameter for consumers needing independent copies

**3. `keep_ref_on_recursion` handler**
- Built-in `recursion_limit_handler` that leaves `$ref` in place instead of raising `ResolutionError`
- Useful for specs with legitimate recursive types (linked lists, trees)
- Works with any `recursion_limit` — unrolls N levels deep, then preserves the `$ref`

### Benchmark results

**Chain references** (Model_i -> Model_{i-1} -> ... -> Model_0):

| Models | Before | After | Speedup |
|--------|--------|-------|---------|
| 10 | 4.0ms | 2.3ms | 1.7x |
| 20 | 260ms | 4.0ms | **65x** |
| 30 | 60,443ms | 6.7ms | **9,022x** |
| 100 | impossible | 19ms | — |
| 500 | impossible | 95ms | — |

**Flat references** (many endpoints sharing the same models):

| Models | Before | After | Speedup |
|--------|--------|-------|---------|
| 100 | ~30ms | 8.9ms | 3.4x |
| 500 | ~150ms | 46ms | 3.3x |

The chain-reference case went from **exponential** to **linear** scaling.

### Why not a C extension?

The C extension in #168 targets the same hot paths but introduces significant maintenance burden:
- Manual `Py_INCREF`/`Py_DECREF` reference counting
- Platform-specific build requirements (`python3-devel`, compiler toolchain)
- Harder to audit for correctness and memory safety
- The dominant bottleneck was **algorithmic** (exponential data blowup from deep-copying chained refs) — structural sharing solves this regardless of language

### Structural sharing trade-off

Resolved subtrees that originated from the same `$ref` target are the **same Python object** in memory. This is safe for:
- Serialization (`json.dumps`, `yaml.dump`) — re-emits shared subtrees correctly
- Read-only traversal — the dominant consumer pattern
- Validation — validators only read

If a consumer mutates a shared subtree, the change is visible everywhere it appears. For consumers that need independent copies, use `materialize=True`:

```python
parser = ResolvingParser("spec.yaml", materialize=True)
```

### Open questions

- Are there pathological specs where the resolved-reference cache could produce incorrect results?
- The cache is keyed on `(url_resource, obj_path)` — need to verify this is always a correct identity

## Test plan

- [x] All existing tests pass (92 passed, 6 skipped, 1 xfailed)
- [x] Recursion protection verified (self-ref and mutual recursion)
- [x] `keep_ref_on_recursion` tested with recursion_limit=1 and 2
- [x] `materialize=True` produces independent copies
- [x] Chain benchmark: linear scaling verified up to 500 models

## Summary by Sourcery

Optimize reference resolution performance while preserving pure-Python implementation, adding structural sharing, caching, and optional materialization for safety.

New Features:
- Add optional materialize flag to reference resolution to allow consumers to request independent deep-copied subtrees.
- Introduce keep_ref_on_recursion handler to preserve $ref entries when recursion limits are hit instead of raising errors.
- Provide an optional fast deepcopy backend using orjson via a new fast extra dependency.
- Add a profiling script for the resolver to benchmark and analyze performance on different spec shapes.

Bug Fixes:
- Correct path_get to return falsy values at the root path instead of incorrectly falling back to the default value.

Enhancements:
- Rework path_get and path_set to use iterative, type-specialized fast paths for dicts and lists, with ABC-based fallbacks for other collection types.
- Add internal cache and structural sharing to RefResolver dereferencing to avoid redundant deep copies and reduce complexity on chained references.
- Refactor partial resolution to apply reference substitutions via direct path replacement rather than using path_set.
- Replace generator-based reference_iterator with an explicit stack-based traversal over container types for better performance.

Build:
- Add orjson as an optional fast extra in pyproject.toml for improved deepcopy performance when available.

Tests:
- Extend path_get tests to cover behavior with falsy values and default handling.

items.title: Fix unaligned distance metadata loads [MOD-15303]
items.body:
## Summary
- load SQ8, INT8, and UINT8 trailing FP32 metadata through alignment-safe helpers in scalar and SIMD kernels
- make integer normalization and test/reference metadata access alignment-safe
- repair the SQ8-FP32 benchmark's storage/query argument order and array teardown
- add explicit odd-dimension SQ8-FP32 regression coverage

## Root cause
Trailing FP32 metadata follows byte-width vector payloads. For dimensions not divisible by four, casting `payload + dimension` to `float *` creates a misaligned pointer and undefined behavior. The SQ8-FP32 benchmark also supplied its FP32 query and SQ8 storage in reverse order, producing an out-of-bounds read.

## Impact
Odd-dimensional SQ8/SQ8-FP32 and INT8/UINT8 cosine distance calculations no longer rely on misaligned FP32 loads, including dispatched SIMD implementations and strict-alignment architectures.

## Validation
- `./check-format.sh`
- alignment/undefined sanitizer: 520 SQ8/SQ8-FP32/INT8/UINT8 distance tests
- alignment/undefined sanitizer: affected component, INT8, UINT8, and index utility tests
- AddressSanitizer + undefined sanitizer: SQ8-FP32 dimension-100 benchmark matrix (available AVX2-FMA, AVX2, SSE4, and scalar paths)

### Deterministic alignment regression proof

Built the regression test with Clang 18.1.8 and fatal AddressSanitizer/alignment sanitization:

- PR `c724d32b`: exited `0`; `SpacesTest.SQ8_FP32_odd_dim_unaligned_metadata_test` passed.
- Main `dd6879e8`, with only the test and safe reference-helper changes applied: exited `1`.
- UBSan reported the old production load in `SQ8_FP32_InnerProduct_Impl`:

```text
src/VecSim/spaces/IP/IP.cpp:61:27:
runtime error: load of misaligned address 0x503000025691
for type 'const float', which requires 4 byte alignment
```

The forced address ends in `...691`, proving it is not four-byte aligned. The sanitizer stack traces the failure from `SQ8_FP32_InnerProduct_Impl` directly to the odd-dimension regression test.

Jira: [MOD-15303](https://redislabs.atlassian.net/browse/MOD-15303)

items.title: CLUSTER and MERGE split contained intervals into separate clusters — Closes #214
items.body:
## Summary

`CLUSTER` and `MERGE` (which composes on `CLUSTER`) produced incorrect results when an interval is fully contained within an earlier, wider interval. They decided cluster boundaries with `CASE WHEN LAG("end") OVER (...) >= "start"` — comparing each interval to the *immediately preceding* row's end rather than the running maximum end of the cluster so far. When a wide interval contains a later narrower one, a subsequent interval that still overlaps the wide one (but not the narrow predecessor) was spuriously split into a new cluster.

For `[0,100),[10,20),[30,40)`, GIQL `MERGE` returned `[0,100),[30,40)` (wrong) vs the bedtools/bioframe oracle's `[0,100)`. On a 1e6 interval set `MERGE` returned 847,897 regions vs the oracle's 844,107 (~0.5% wrongly split). Contained intervals are common in real genomic data (genes over exons, broad peaks over narrow sub-peaks).

The fix keys the boundary flag off the **running maximum end** of the preceding rows — `MAX("end") OVER (PARTITION BY chrom ORDER BY start ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING)` — the cluster's true right edge so far. The distance offset, first-row NULL behavior, and the separate `PREV()` predecessor-reference predicate are unchanged; non-containment inputs are unaffected (the running max equals `LAG` when nothing is contained). Verified: containment now yields the single correct region, and the 1e6 set returns exactly 844,107 (oracle match), at similar/better runtime (0.26s vs 0.43s).

Discovered by the benchmark suite via a row-count discrepancy against the bedtools/bioframe oracle.

Closes #214

## Proposed changes

- **fix** — `src/giql/expanders/cluster.py`: the adjacency-flag window becomes a running-max `MAX("end")` framed window instead of `LAG("end")`; docstring updated.
- **test** — Update the transpilation assertions (`test_cluster.py`, `test_genomic_columns.py`, `test_cluster_predicate_transpilation.py`, `test_expander.py`) from the `LAG` shape to the `MAX(...) OVER (... ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING)` shape, and add containment cases to the bedtools `CLUSTER` and `MERGE` oracle suites.

## Test cases

| # | Test Suite | Given | When | Then | Coverage Target |
|---|------------|-------|------|------|-----------------|
| 1 | bedtools `test_merge` | A wide interval containing a later narrower one that ends before a third still-contained interval | `MERGE` is executed | Output matches the single bedtools merge region | Containment merge |
| 2 | bedtools `test_cluster` | Same containment shape | `CLUSTER` is executed | All three share one cluster id, matching the single bedtools region | Containment cluster |
| 3 | `TestClusterExpander` | A CLUSTER with/without a distance | Transpiled | Emits the `MAX("end") OVER (... ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND 1 PRECEDING)` boundary (with `+ distance` when positive) | Boundary window SQL |

Full non-integration suite (1112 passed) and the bedtools CLUSTER/MERGE oracle (13 passed, incl. the two new containment cases) stay green.

items.title: docs(decision): ESQuery-selector pilot — measured, not adopting
items.body:
Phase 4 / ESQuery pilot, gated on the roadmap's "measure before adopting".

**Result: do not adopt broadly.** A decision record (`docs/decisions/esquery-selector-pilot.md`), no code change.

Empirically on napi 0.44:
- ✅ The selectors (`>`, descendant, `:has`, `:not`, `:is`) work in the JS rule API.
- 🚩 But `find`/`findAll` search **all descendants**, and `>` can't anchor to the scope root — so swapping a direct-children walk over-matches nested declarations (a nested class's `extends` attributed to the outer). Correctness hazard.
- ⏱️ No perf win: TS heritage extraction over 120 files (×30) was ~1.1× **slower** with ESQuery.

Keep the manual walks (clearer scope, correct, marginally faster). ESQuery stays available for new descendant/`:has` queries where that's genuinely what's wanted.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

---

<!-- kody-pr-summary:start -->
This pull request adds a new decision document detailing the outcome of a pilot program to evaluate the adoption of ESQuery-style structural selectors in `@ast-grep/napi`.

The document, `docs/decisions/esquery-selector-pilot.md`, concludes that ESQuery selectors should **not** be broadly adopted to replace existing direct-children walks.

Key findings from the pilot:
- ESQuery selectors work in the JS API.
- **Correctness hazard**: Descendant semantics in ESQuery selectors can over-match, leading to incorrect results for scoped searches compared to manual direct-child walks.
- **No performance benefit**: Benchmarking showed ESQuery selectors to be marginally slower (approximately 10%) than manual walks.

Based on these findings, the decision is to **not migrate** existing direct-children walks. The document also outlines specific scenarios where ESQuery selectors might still be valuable for new queries.

items.title: fix: remove the static planner SortMergeJoinExec broadcast conversion
items.body:
# Which issue does this PR close?

Partially addresses #2046 (q4 and q78 only).

# Rationale for this change

TL;DR. The SMJ "broadcast join" optimization in the static planner was poorly thought out. TPC-DS tests exposed that it caused correctness issues. Let's remove it.

This PR does not make any changes to AQE join selection.

# AI description of changes

`54.0.0` added a static-planner rewrite that converted a `SortMergeJoinExec` with a small build side into a broadcast `CollectLeft` hash join, gated by `ballista.optimizer.broadcast_sort_merge_join_enabled` (default `true`). The rewrite produces incorrect results, so the only safe value for the key is `false`. A config knob whose correct setting is always "off" is better removed along with the code it gates.

This is not an edge-case path. Ballista sets `datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = false` by default (#1648), so joins are planned as `SortMergeJoinExec` unless a user opts out, and the conversion then fired on any join with a side under the threshold.

# What changes are included in this PR?

- Remove `convert_sort_merge_to_hash_join` and its `strip_sort` helper from `DefaultDistributedPlanner`. A `SortMergeJoinExec` is no longer a broadcast candidate; only a `HashJoinExec(Partitioned)` is.
- Remove the `ballista.optimizer.broadcast_sort_merge_join_enabled` config key and its `BallistaConfig` accessor.
- Drop the test asserting the conversion happens, and the test asserting the threshold gated it (now vacuous). `distributed_sort_merge_join_unchanged_when_flag_disabled` becomes `distributed_sort_merge_join_is_never_broadcast`, since that is now unconditional behavior.
- Re-enable TPC-DS q4 and q78 in the correctness gate.
- Add a `55.0.0` upgrade guide; drop the stale "not been released yet" note from the `54.0.0` guide.

Broadcast promotion of a `HashJoinExec` under `ballista.optimizer.broadcast_join_threshold_bytes` is unchanged, as is the correctness guard that demotes a DataFusion-promoted `CollectLeft` join with an unsafe join type.

# Are there any user-facing changes?

Yes, two, both documented in `docs/source/upgrading/55.0.0.md`:

1. `ballista.optimizer.broadcast_sort_merge_join_enabled` no longer exists. Ballista rejects unknown configuration keys, so a session that still sets it now fails with ``configuration key `optimizer.broadcast_sort_merge_join_enabled` does not exist``. This is a breaking config change against `54.0.0`.
2. A `SortMergeJoinExec` is never converted to a broadcast join. Because sort-merge is Ballista's default join strategy, join plan shape — and therefore performance and shuffle behavior — changes on upgrade for any query with a join whose smaller side is under `10 MB`. Users who want the broadcast can set `datafusion.optimizer.prefer_hash_join = true`, at the cost of opting into the non-spilling hash join for all joins in the session.

## Verification

Locally: `cargo clippy --all-targets --workspace --all-features -- -D warnings` passes, and the `ballista-scheduler` planner, `ballista-core` config, and `tpcds` bin tests pass.

The q4/q78 fix itself is **not** verified locally — it needs SF1 TPC-DS data and a live cluster. The TPC-DS SF1 workflow runs on this PR and is the real check; if q4 or q78 still diverge, those skip entries should go back with an updated reason.

Given the default-plan-shape change, TPC-H benchmark numbers before/after would be worth having before this merges.

items.title: perf: accelerate embedding hybrid search with optional numpy BLAS
items.body:
## Summary
- Optional numpy BLAS path for the Python embedding-search fallback: process-level `(N, D)` matrix cache keyed on a WAL-aware DB stamp; score via `matrix @ q / norms`; invalidate on write/delete.
- Keep pure-Python cosine as no-numpy fallback (`DAGAYN_EMBEDDING_SEARCH_BACKEND=python` / `auto`); `dagayn[numpy]` is optional only.
- Document already-shipped EmbeddingStore pinning and batched `embed_nodes`; update PERFORMANCE WIP §4.5 and LOCAL-EMBEDDINGS.

Closes #16

## Test plan
- [x] Ranking parity + pin-reuse + matrix-cache tests on agent
- [x] Microbench (`5000×128`): numpy path much faster than pure-Python; Rust remains default
- [ ] Confirm search works without numpy installed
- [ ] ruff clean on touched files

<!-- CURSOR_SUMMARY -->
---

> [!NOTE]
> **Medium Risk**
> Changes hybrid semantic search behavior on the Python/auto fallback path (ranking and caching), though parity tests mitigate regressions; incorrect cache invalidation could serve stale results after embedding updates.
> 
> **Overview**
> When `DAGAYN_EMBEDDING_SEARCH_BACKEND` is `python` or `auto` falls back from Rust, **`EmbeddingStore.search`** no longer always scans rows with an inline pure-Python cosine loop. It routes through **`_python_embedding_search`**: if numpy is installed (`pip install "dagayn[numpy]"`), it loads provider vectors into a process-level **`float32 (N, D)`** matrix cached by **`(db_path, provider, WAL-aware stamp)`**, scores with **`matrix @ q / row_norms`**, and uses **`argpartition(k-1)`** for top-k. Without numpy, behavior stays the **batched pure-Python** path.
> 
> **Cache invalidation** runs after embedding **writes** (`embed_nodes`), **per-node** retries, **`remove_node`**, and **orphan deletes** so stale matrices are not reused.
> 
> Packaging adds optional **`numpy`** extra (also in **`dev`** / **`all`**). **`embeddings.py`** re-exports cache helpers for tests and monkeypatching. Docs (**README**, **LOCAL-EMBEDDINGS**, **PERFORMANCE §4.5**) and **CHANGELOG** describe the shipped path; **`tools/embedding_search_benchmark.py`** gains **`--compare-numpy`**. Tests cover ranking parity, top-k boundary correctness, matrix-cache reuse, and a soft numpy-vs-Python speed check; **`test_search`** adds **`_get_cached_emb_store`** pin-reuse coverage.

items.title: Fix critical bugs in box parsing, coordinate handling, and model inference
items.body:
## Summary

This PR fixes multiple critical bugs across the CXR grounding benchmark that caused silent failures, incorrect results, and crashes. The changes include:

1. **Extraction of shared utilities** into a new `cxr_common.py` module to eliminate code duplication and fix bugs in image loading and box parsing
2. **Critical box parsing fixes** that were causing complete detection failures for some models
3. **Coordinate handling improvements** including proper clamping and tolerance for floating-point rounding
4. **Model-specific inference fixes** for RadVLM, CheXagent, MAIRA-2, and BioViL-T
5. **HPC deployment infrastructure** with setup scripts and job templates

## Key Changes

### Core Fixes in `cxr_common.py` (new file)

- **Normalized-scale box detection** (HIGH IMPACT): Changed from all-or-nothing `all(0.0 <= v <= 1.0)` check to a `-0.05 <= v <= 1.05` tolerance band with per-coordinate clamping. This fixes a real bug where boxes like `[0.1, 0.2, 1.02, 0.95]` (plausible float-rounding artifacts) would fail detection entirely and be misinterpreted as raw pixel coordinates, producing degenerate 1×1 boxes.

- **Removed unreachable 0-1000 scale heuristic**: The condition `max(vals) > img_w and max(vals) > img_h` could never fire correctly for MIMIC-CXR images (2000-3000px), making this dead code that would misinterpret coordinates if it ever did execute.

- **Added coordinate clamping**: Boxes straddling image edges are now clamped to `[0, img_w] × [0, img_h]` before returning, preventing out-of-range coordinates from reaching downstream consumers.

- **Guarded `box_iou()` against degenerate boxes**: Now explicitly returns `0.0` if either box has area ≤ 0, preventing nonsensical IoU values.

- **Multi-frame color DICOM support**: Added explicit handling for 4D pixel arrays `(frames, H, W, samples)` before the grayscale multi-frame check.

- **Unified image loader**: Consolidated six duplicate implementations with improved DICOM handling (RescaleSlope/Intercept, VOI LUT, MONOCHROME1 inversion, truncated JPEG tolerance).

### Model-Specific Fixes

- **RadVLM** (`radvlm_medsam.py`):
  - Fixed prompt-response parsing: replaced fragile `re.split(r"(user|assistant)", ...)` (case-sensitive, substring-vulnerable) with token-space slicing by prompt length
  - Moved to shared `parse_box_from_response()` from `cxr_common.py`

- **CheXagent** (`chexagent_medsam.py`):
  - Fixed box parsing regex to recognize CheXagent's actual output format: `<|box|> (x1,y1),(x2,y2) <|/box|>` with 0-100 scale (verified against RadVLM authors' own evaluation harness)
  - Previous regex patterns could never match this format, causing 100% detection failure
  - Moved to shared parser with CheXagent tag format checked first

- **MAIRA-2** (`maira2_medsam.py`):
  - Fixed silent discarding of multiple boxes per phrase: now takes union (smallest enclosing box) of all returned boxes instead of `boxes[0]` only
  - Added `union_box()` helper to `cxr_common.py`

- **BioViL-T** (`biovilt_medsam.py`):
  - Fixed off-by-one in connected-component bounding box: changed `xs.max()` to `xs.max() + 1` to use exclusive upper bounds (matching gold boxes and all other models)

items.body: I hereby agree to the terms of the CLA available at: https://docs.databend.com/dev/policies/cla/ ## Summary The bloom runtime filter's probe-side column reference was resolved using the `ColumnBinding.column_name`, which is the query-context name and can be an alias. When a column alias collides with another physical column name in the same table, `schema.index_of(name)` finds the wrong column. This causes the bloom filter to read unrelated data (default-filled zeros or wrong column values), reject all probe rows, and produce incorrect join results. **Minimal reproduction:** ```sql CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE t_probe(col_a INT NOT NULL, col_b INT NOT NULL) row_per_block = 5; CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE t_build(col_a INT NOT NULL); INSERT INTO t_probe VALUES (100,1),(101,2),(102,3),(103,4),(104,5),(200,6),(201,7),(202,8),(203,9),(204,10),(300,11),(301,12),(302,13),(303,14),(304,15),(400,16),(401,17),(402,18),(403,19),(404,20); INSERT INTO t_build VALUES (1),(2),(3); SET enable_join_runtime_filter = 1; SELECT count() FROM t_build AS b INNER JOIN (SELECT col_b AS col_a FROM t_probe) AS p ON b.col_a = p.col_a; -- Expected: 3 -- Bug: 0 (bloom RF resolves "col_a" to the physical col_a instead of the aliased col_b) ``` **Fix:** In `project_column_ref`, look up the physical column name from the table schema via `column_id` instead of using the binding's context name. ## Tests - [ ] Unit Test - [x] Logic Test - [ ] Benchmark Test - [ ] No Test ## Type of change - [x] Bug Fix (non-breaking change which fixes an issue) - [ ] New Feature (non-breaking change which adds functionality) - [ ] Breaking Change (fix or feature that could cause existing functionality not to work as expected) - [ ] Documentation Update - [ ] Refactoring - [ ] Performance Improvement - [ ] Other (please describe): - - - This change is [](https://reviewable.io/reviews/databendlabs/databend/20105)

items.title: fix(codegen): round JS arithmetic to f64 at every i32-chain step (#7232)
items.body:
Fixes #7232.

## The bug

```ts
let s0 = 12345;
let s1 = (s0 * 1103515245 + 12345) & 0x7fffffff;
let s2 = (s1 * 1103515245 + 12345) & 0x7fffffff;   // node 654583808, perry 654583775
```

An LCG step. Wrong straight-line and loop-carried; correct through a function
boundary. No throw, no warning — just different numbers, in PRNG seeds, hash
mixing and checksum accumulators.

## Root cause

`crates/perry-codegen/src/expr/i32_fast_path.rs`. The i32-native fast path
evaluated the whole chain in exact two's-complement `mul/add i32`:

```llvm
%r4 = mul i32 %r3, 1103515245
%r5 = add i32 %r4, 12345
%r6 = and i32 %r5, 2147483647
```

ECMAScript numbers are IEEE-754 doubles, so `*` and `+` round their result to
the nearest double **before** the next operator runs. `1406932606 *
1103515245` is ~2^61 — past 2^53, where the double's ulp is 256 — so Node's
mask reads a *rounded* product while the exact `mul i32` reads the low bits the
double had already discarded. It only reproduced through a local because a
function boundary NaN-boxes the intermediate, which rounds it.

The old admission rule (`can_lower_expr_as_i32`) required only that every
integer **literal** fit in i32. That is neither necessary — `Math.imul` is
*defined* as an exact low-32 multiply and needs no such rule — nor sufficient:
`1103515245` fits in i32, and its product with an i32-range local does not fit
in a double.

## The invariant

> An i32-native chain computes the exact two's-complement low 32 bits of the
> integer result. JS evaluates the same chain in doubles, rounding at every
> operator. The two agree **only while every intermediate is exactly
> representable as a double** — `|v| <= 2^53`. Below that ceiling the JS double
> *is* the exact integer, so `low32(exact) == ToInt32(double)`; above it, they
> are different numbers.

So the predicate now carries a magnitude bound through the whole chain
(`i32_chain_magnitude_bits`), capped at 53. `Add`/`Sub` grow the bound by one
bit and `Mul` sums it — the same composition `known_finite_magnitude_bits`
already used for the `toint32_fast` poison proof, with 53 in place of 63
because this bound gates *exact integer arithmetic*, not one `fptosi`. The cap
applies to `Add`/`Sub` too, not only `Mul`: two ceiling-width products sum to
2^54.

Both emitters of the chain consult the same function, so the gate and the
last-resort arithmetic arm in `lower_expr_native_i32` cannot drift apart.

## Keeping the fast path fast

A naive 53-bit cap deoptimizes a lot of correct code, so the bound is measured
rather than assumed:

* an integer literal contributes its own bit width (`h * 31` is 37 bits, not 64);
* `x & m` with a non-negative literal mask lands in `[0, m]`;
* `x >> k` / `x >>> k` by a literal `k` drop `k` bits;
* a `const` bound to a numeric literal contributes *its* width — this is what
  keeps the dominant strided-index shape `buf[y * WIDTH + x]` exact;
* `Math.imul` is exempt entirely.

Measured over all 30 programs in `benchmarks/suite/`, comparing emitted LLVM IR
byte-for-byte against `main`: **29 are unchanged**. The one that moves is
`11_prime_sieve`, whose `for (let j = i * i; ...)` preheader is genuinely
unbounded and now rounds — one `mul i32` becomes `fmul` + `fjcvtzs`, executed
once per outer-loop iteration.

Two of those 29 took a detour worth recording, because both are cases where the
first attempt at this fix *did* regress them:

* `bench_int_arithmetic` lost half its `mul i32` (108 → 54) until the const
  literal's own width was measured — `const SIZE = 100` was reading as the
  32-bit default, so the convolution index `(y - 1) * SIZE + (x - 1)` came out
  at 65 bits.
* `bench_typed_array_untyped_access` (the #5525 Blowfish guard) turned a native
  `lshr` into a `js_dynamic_ushr` call, because the exactness proof had been
  applied to the last-resort *bitwise* arm as well. Bitwise operators are
  ToInt32-wrapped by definition and cannot leave the exact range; that arm is
  where bcryptjs's `S[l >>> 24]` lands with an untyped operand, and it must
  stay proof-free.

## Red then green

`test-files/test_gap_7232_i32_chain_double_rounding.ts` — the issue's three
shapes (straight-line, loop-carried, through-a-call), every ToInt32-shaped
consumer, compound assignment, the unmasked product, a full LCG run, the
2^53 boundary from both sides, and the chains that must *stay* exact
(`h * 31 + c`, FNV-1a via `Math.imul`, 16×16 masked mixing, `i * cols + j`
indices, `i * i`).

* Unfixed `main`: 4 lines diverge from `node --experimental-strip-types` 26.5.1.
* Fixed: byte-identical.

Fourteen unit tests in `crates/perry-codegen/src/expr/i32_fast_path/bits_tests.rs`
pin the bound itself, and are sabotage-checked both ways: widening
`F64_EXACT_INTEGER_BITS` past 53 reds the four divergence tests; deleting the
`BitAnd`/shift/const tightening reds the four exactness tests.

## Gates

* `cargo test -p perry-codegen --lib` — 540 pass.
* Gap suite, oracle-exact against the pinned Node.
* `compiler_output_regression.py census --gate` — green, no floor touched, no
  `--update`.
* `cargo fmt --all`; file-size cap offender list unchanged (16), and no file in
  this diff is on it.
* No GC-adjacent codegen touched, so the GC matrix does not apply — the diff is
  confined to `expr/i32_fast_path.rs` plus the mechanical argument threading at
  its call sites.

## Summary by CodeRabbit

* **Bug Fixes**
  * Fixed incorrect results caused by double rounding in chained 32-bit integer arithmetic.
  * Improved accuracy near the `2^53` precision boundary across arithmetic, loops, assignments, indexing, and function calls.
  * Preserved exact behavior for bitwise operations and `Math.imul`.

* **Performance**
  * Expanded optimized integer handling for constant numeric values in arrays, buffers, typed arrays, collections, and related operations.

* **Tests**
  * Added comprehensive regression and boundary coverage for arithmetic precision and integer fast paths.

items.title: Fix GEMM BLAS handle sharing across threads
items.body:
Use a thread-local BLAS handle for CUDA GEMM so concurrent worker threads, such as tensor-parallel ranks, do not race while setting streams on a shared handle.

## Summary

<!--
A concise description of **what** this PR changes. Prefer bullet points over
prose. Reference files with backtick-fenced paths (e.g. `src/cuda/gemm/blas.h`).
-->

- Use a `thread_local` BLAS handle in `src/native/cuda/ops/gemm/blas.h`.
- Avoid sharing one CUDA BLAS handle across concurrent host threads when tensor-parallel ranks execute GEMM on different streams/devices.

## Motivation

<!--
Explain **why** this change is needed. Link to any related issue, bug, or
discussion. If this is a performance change, include before/after numbers
(hardware, shape, dtype, and the measurement methodology).
-->

CUDA GEMM currently uses a process-wide static BLAS handle. In multi-threaded inference, such as tensor-parallel execution where each rank runs in its own worker thread, concurrent GEMM calls can race while setting streams on the shared handle.

This can produce incorrect results in multi-GPU tensor-parallel inference even when single-GPU inference works correctly. Making the handle `thread_local` gives each worker thread its own BLAS handle and avoids cross-thread stream mutation.

## Why

The NVIDIA/skills sync workflow **drops any skill missing `skill-card.md`, `skill.oms.sig`, or an eval dataset** — the enforcement step removes the skill dir before the PR is created, so non-compliant skills never merge into the catalog. The same requirement is tracked as `SRC-11` in `bionemo-agent-toolkit`'s CONTRIBUTING.

State of this repo against those three artifacts:

| Artifact | Status |
|---|---|
| eval dataset | present — 11 functional tasks + 2 trigger cases under `evals/` |
| `skill-card.md` | **this PR** |
| `skill.oms.sig` | outstanding — needs `nvskills-ci` wired here (see below) |

## What's in the card

Description, owner, license, use case, requirements (nvMolKit install, CUDA GPU, RDKit interop), risks and mitigations, references, output types, evaluation, and ethical considerations.

The risk section is specific to what this skill actually is — a code-authoring skill. It covers incorrect API usage producing silently wrong cheminformatics results, numerical divergence from RDKit for stochastic operations (ETKDG, force-field optimization), GPU memory exhaustion on large batched runs, and misuse of the asynchronous result model (`AsyncGpuResult` / `Device3DResult`) yielding partial data.

**Evaluation results are marked pending, not fabricated.** NVSkills-Eval has not been run against this skill; the card states the eval task counts that exist and says results and a `BENCHMARK.md` will follow.

`skill.oms.sig` cannot be added by a PR — it is emitted by the `NVIDIA/nvskills-ci` service. Wiring it here needs a `request-nvskills-ci.yml` workflow, the `NVSKILLS_CI_DISPATCH_TOKEN` secret, and a maintainer commenting `/nvskills-ci` on a PR. This repo already has CI workflows, so it is the smallest lift of the three source repos. Happy to open that as a follow-up.

## Context

`bionemo-agent-toolkit` vendors this skill via `components.d/nvmolkit.yml` and rsyncs with `--delete`, so a card committed there is wiped on the next nightly sync. This repo is the source of truth. The catalog carries an interim copy of this same card in a `compliance.d/` overlay, which is retired automatically once this merges.
